name: load-bearing
title: Load-bearing vocabulary (louisabraham)
description:
One rule, measuring how far a document's vocabulary spreads across the words that mark out AI writing. The list comes from github.com/louisabraham/load-bearing, which sorts GitHub pull request descriptions into ten groups by vocabulary alone; one group grew from under 1 per cent of them in January 2025 to 37 per cent by August 2026.

It updates itself: tools/load-bearing.mjs rebuilds it from upstream daily. (pr-vocabulary re-derives its own list from the same raw material, by a related method.) Nothing upstream is labelled, though. There are no human and AI classes in it, only ten clusters and the timing of one, and its authors say the group is mostly Claude with no guarantee. Every human and AI number on the rule is this repo's own audit corpus, not theirs.

rules.name: Vocabulary spread across the arriving group
rules.description: AI writing draws on a recognisable vocabulary. This counts how many different words from that vocabulary a document uses. No single word is a tell, and the list holds ordinary ones like nothing, half and asked; it is the spread across the list that fires the rule. The words are from github.com/louisabraham/load-bearing, which measured 461,000 GitHub pull request descriptions.
rules.suggest: No one word here is wrong, so do not walk the list swapping them out. The finding names every word that counted: rewrite the passages carrying the most of them, in words you would have chosen yourself, until the rate falls. Trading each flagged word for the same favourite synonym swaps one shared vocabulary for another.
rules.note: Each word counts once however often it appears, so a document that genuinely needs one pays for it once and only breadth accumulates. The total is divided by the square root of the length rather than by the length, because a count of distinct things saturates as a document grows: dividing by length made the score fall with length, -0.52 against log length over 80 human documents where the root gives -0.00. Wire copy and forum writing sit highest among the human documents, because the list carries ordinary reporting verbs. Weighting the words by how characteristic each is was tried four ways, including upstream's own per-word log-odds, and every one selected the same documents.
rules.evidence: At 1.2 distinct words per root word: 1 of 80 human documents, 17 of 18 AI documents. Independently corroborated: every one of the 1,198 words carries a higher rate in pull request descriptions that identify themselves as machine-written than in those that do not, median 3.19 times, measured over 96,170 signed and 370,641 unsigned descriptions. The group upstream picks without ever reading a signature comes out 46 per cent signed, against under 5 per cent for most of the other nine.

reference.unit: distinct list words per square root of length
reference.human: median 0.70, p75 0.86, p90 0.97, p95 1.11, max 1.41 over 80 documents. Research papers and reference material lowest, wire copy and forum writing highest.
reference.ai: median 1.39, min 0.85, p25 1.31, max 1.91 over 18 documents.
reference.tune: Raise it for wire copy, forum writing and anything narrating a decision. Lower it for reference material and specifications, which sit near 0.5.

hit:
The proposal rests on a premise nobody has stated plainly, and the review board should say so before it votes. The claim is that the current interface carries the whole of the scheduling behaviour, and that replacing it is therefore a contained change. That claim was asserted rather than measured. When the timings were finally taken, the picture that survived was the opposite of the one in the summary: the interface handles about a third of the work, and the remainder sits in two helpers that nobody has touched since the fourth release.

Two halves of the migration were handed to different teams, and neither half settles the question alone. The first team drew a boundary at the queue and stopped. The second team assumed the boundary was elsewhere and built against it. Both were working honestly from the same document, which quietly leaves the seam undefined. The disagreement between them is load-bearing, and papering over it in the status report is worse than leaving it open, because a reader now believes a question was settled that was never asked.

What is owed to the reviewers is a plain account of what is known. Eleven of the fourteen benchmarks were re-measured after the change and came back within noise of the numbers taken before it. Two got worse, by amounts that are small but consistent across repeated runs. The last one was refused outright by the harness and has not been investigated. Nothing in the write-up mentions the refusal, and the summary table shows thirteen rows where there should be fourteen.

The ceiling the design sets is narrower than the machinery beneath it can honour. That is not a defect in the implementation; it is a decision that was made early, deliberately, and for reasons that were good at the time and have gone stale since. Whoever revisits it should know that the constraint predates the current traffic pattern by three years. The asymmetry it introduces between reads and writes is genuine, and it will not be argued away.

None of this makes the migration a bad idea. It makes the estimate wrong. The work that stands between here and a shipped change is roughly twice what the plan admits, and the plan gains nothing by holding the smaller figure. A revised estimate that is honest about the two helpers, the undefined seam and the refused benchmark is worth more to the people deciding than a confident one that quietly omits them. The reviewers can then judge the trade for themselves, which is what they are there for, and the decision that follows will rest on something that holds.

The schedule attached to the proposal assumes the review completes in a single round. Reviews of this size have taken two or three rounds in each of the last four quarters, and there is no reason to expect this one to behave differently. Adding a second round moves the delivery date into the following quarter, which changes who has to be told and when. That is a conversation to have now rather than in six weeks.

There is a version of this change that is genuinely contained, and it is worth describing because it may be the right one. Leave the two helpers where they are, move only the queue boundary, and accept that the seam stays undefined for another release. That version is smaller than the one on the table, it carries less risk, and it does not require the estimate to be revised. What it does not do is deliver the throughput number the proposal opens with, and the reviewers should be told that plainly rather than discovering it in the following quarter's report when the number has quietly moved.

None of the three reviewers has asked for the raw timings, and the raw timings are where the disagreement lives. They should be attached to the next revision whether or not anybody asks, because a reader who wants to check the claim currently cannot, and a claim that cannot be checked is worth less than one that is simply stated without numbers at all.

Release 4.2.0

Added support for PostgreSQL 17. Added the --jobs flag. Added base64 encoding for binary columns.
Added a .sha256 file beside each table file. Added the compressed field to the manifest.

Fixed a crash when a table name contained a slash. Fixed the timestamp format for columns declared
with time zone. Fixed a memory leak in the compression path. Fixed the exit status for an
unreadable target directory, which was 1 and is now 3.

Changed the default for --jobs from 1 to the core count, capped at 8. Changed the manifest version
from 1 to 2. Changed the log prefix to include the schema name.

Removed the --legacy-quoting flag. Removed support for PostgreSQL 11.

Release 4.1.3

Fixed a regression in numeric formatting that dropped trailing zeros.

Release 4.1.2

Fixed the glob matcher, which treated a leading dot as a literal.
Fixed a race between the manifest write and the directory rename.

Release 4.1.1

Fixed the connection string parser for URIs containing a password with a percent sign.

Release 4.1.0

Added --include and --exclude. Added --views. Added JSON log output via PGEXPORT_LOG_FORMAT.
Fixed enum export, which wrote ordinals instead of labels.
Changed the temporary directory location to sit beside the target.

Release 4.0.0

Rewrote the exporter to hold one snapshot transaction for the whole run.
Removed the resume feature, which could not be made correct under the new transaction model.
Removed the --tables flag in favour of --include.
Changed the manifest from CSV to JSON.
Changed checksums from MD5 to SHA-256.
Added the schema file.
Added atomic directory rename.

Release 3.6.2

Fixed a deadlock when two exports ran against the same database.

Release 3.6.1

Fixed quoting for values containing a carriage return.

Release 3.6.0

Added --gzip. Added the rows field to the manifest. Fixed the column order for tables with a
composite primary key, which did not follow the key definition.

Release 3.5.0

Added support for materialised views. Fixed date formatting before 1000 AD.
Changed the log level names from numbers to text.

Release 3.4.1

Fixed a crash on empty tables.

Release 3.4.0

Added the schema field to each manifest table entry.
Fixed array export for multidimensional arrays.
Removed the undocumented --debug flag.

Release 3.3.0

Added PGEXPORT_TMPDIR. Added the bytes field to the manifest.
Fixed the checksum for compressed files, which covered the compressed bytes.
Changed --quiet to suppress per-table lines rather than all output.

Release 3.2.1

Fixed a file descriptor leak when a table export failed midway.

Release 3.2.0

Added --no-snapshot for engines without repeatable read.
Added a progress line every thirty seconds for slow tables.
Fixed domain columns, which exported as text regardless of the underlying type.

Release 3.1.0

Added composite type support in record literal syntax.
Fixed the manifest timestamp, which used local time instead of UTC.
Removed the --format flag, which had only one accepted value.

Release 3.0.1

Fixed a crash when the target directory existed and was empty.

Release 3.0.0

Changed the on-disk layout to one file per table.
Changed the header row to always be present, including for empty tables.
Removed the single-file export mode.
Added the manifest.

Release 2.4.2

Fixed sequence handling, which is now documented as out of scope.

Release 2.4.1

Fixed a parse error on connection strings without a port.

Release 2.4.0

Added --verbose. Added the elapsed time to each completion line.
Fixed boolean formatting, which wrote t and f.

Release 2.3.0

Added --include and --exclude as an alternative to listing tables positionally.
Fixed the column type for citext, which exported as bytea.
Changed the default target from the current directory to a required argument.

Release 2.2.1

Fixed a hang when the server closed the connection during a large table.

Release 2.2.0

Added support for PostgreSQL 14. Added the created field to the manifest.
Fixed interval formatting, which used the server locale.
Removed support for PostgreSQL 9.6.

Release 2.1.0

Added checksums. Added the --check subcommand to verify an export against its checksums.
Fixed numeric export for values wider than 38 digits.

Release 2.0.0

Rewrote the connection layer on libpq.
Changed the quoting rules to follow RFC 4180.
Removed the --delimiter flag; the delimiter is now always a comma.

Release 1.4.0

Added --gzip as an experimental flag.
Fixed a crash on tables with no primary key, which now export in physical order.
